chapters.title: Your first quantum experiment
chapters.question: If you run the same program twice, why might it give you two different answers?
chapters.activity: Leave the code as it is and run one shot. Write down the result. Then run 64 shots and look at how often each answer appears.
chapters.objective: Run a program that returns a single bit. By the end, you will be able to explain why its answer can change from one run to the next, and how one extra gate can make the answer predictable.
trace: Each shot starts with photon in state 0. The first Hadamard gate, hadamard(photon), prepares a superposition with equal amplitudes for 0 and 1. The probability of each outcome is the squared magnitude of its amplitude.

With readInX set to false, measure(photon) returns one bit. Each outcome has a 50% chance, even when phaseFlip(photon) changes the sign of the amplitude for 1. Squaring removes that sign. At 64 shots, the program prepares and measures 64 fresh qubits, so the counts can differ from 32 and 32.

Set readInX to true and a second Hadamard acts before measurement. It adds the two amplitudes for outcome 0 and takes their difference for outcome 1. With equal magnitudes, one of those combinations cancels. The sign introduced by the phase flip decides which outcome survives.
chapters.exercise: Set Shots back to 1 and turn readInX on. Leave addPhase on for the first run. Before you click Run, write down your prediction. Run a few times, then change only addPhase to false and repeat. Which setting consistently returns true? Explain why you needed the second H to tell the settings apart.
chapters.hint: The second H combines the two amplitudes. For false it adds them. For true it subtracts the second from the first. In each case, ask whether two equal numbers with those signs cancel.
chapters.solution: With addPhase on, the amplitudes reaching the second H have opposite signs. Their sum is zero, so false has zero probability and the result is always true. With addPhase off, the amplitudes have the same sign. Their difference is zero, so true has zero probability and the result is always false. With readInX off, neither combination takes place. Both settings then give a 50% chance of true.
chapters.oral: A friend says, “I could get the same counts by preparing one photon and measuring it 64 times.” What would you tell them?
chapters.reason: In this program, each shot prepares the state and applies the gates again. With direct readout, every fresh preparation gives another equal chance of false or true. If your friend measures a single prepared qubit, the first result leaves it in the state for that result. Measuring again in the same way, with no gate in between, repeats the first answer.

chapters.title: Numbers and strings
chapters.question: How can moving a single 1 turn the number one into two?
chapters.activity: Read the result in the order [high, low]. Predict what it will show if you turn exchange on, then run the program to check.
chapters.objective: Start with two qubits that spell 01. By the end, you will be able to read that bit string as a number and explain two ways a program can print 10.
trace: Read 01 the way you would read a two-digit number. Each position has a value. In binary, the right position counts ones and the next position counts twos. So 01 means one, while 10 means two. Both strings contain a single 1. Its position tells you what it is worth.

The program names those positions high and low. It prepares high as false (0) and low as true (1). Look at the last line before you run it. It asks for high first and low second, so the result [false, true] spells 01.

Now set exchange to true. The swap gate moves the state of high to low and the state of low to high. The last line still reads the wires in the same order, but this time it finds [true, false]. Open the Circuit tab and follow the two wires through the swap to their measurements.
chapters.exercise: Leave exchange on. Change only the last line so it returns [measure(low), measure(high)]. Before running, write down two predictions. Which qubit now holds 1? Which bit string will you see in Results?
chapters.hint: Follow the 1 through the swap. Then read the names in the return line from left to right.
chapters.solution: The 1 starts on low and moves to high at the swap. The edited return line reads low first, so it gives [false, true], or 01. That is the same output you saw on your first run, even though high now holds the 1.
chapters.oral: You export the original program to Qiskit. How could you check which bit in the output comes from high?
chapters.reason: Use a preparation you can recognize. Set high to true, low to false, and exchange to false. In the Qiskit Python tab, follow the measurement of high into its classical bit, then check where that bit appears in the decoded result. Starting with 00 or 11 would hide a reversal because both positions would look alike.

chapters.title: Linear algebra and interference
chapters.question: Where does the minus sign go when you measure a qubit?
chapters.activity: Compare the two signs first with direct readout, then with a final Hadamard.
chapters.objective: Use two numbers to predict the result of the experiment from Chapter 1. You will see exactly where one of the possible answers disappears.
trace: Write the amplitudes for 0 and 1 as a pair. After the first Hadamard they are (1, 1)/√2. Turning on addPhase changes the second entry to −1/√2. Either pair gives the same direct measurement probabilities because both entries have squared magnitude ½.

Turn on readInX. The final Hadamard adds the entries to find the amplitude for 0 and subtracts the second from the first to find the amplitude for 1, dividing each result by √2. For the pair with the minus sign, the sum is zero. That single cancellation rules out 0.
chapters.exercise: Calculate the output pair of amplitudes for the plus sign. Then test both signs with readInX off and on. Which readout lets you identify the sign from one shot?
chapters.hint: For the plus sign, the sum before the final division is 2/√2. The difference is zero.
chapters.solution: The plus sign gives amplitudes (1, 0) after the last gate, so you always read false. The minus sign gives (0, 1), so you always read true. With direct readout, either preparation can give either bit.
chapters.oral: What would happen if you changed the signs of both amplitudes together?
chapters.reason: Their sum and difference would both change sign. Their squared magnitudes would stay the same. A common phase leaves measurement probabilities unchanged. The sign between the two entries is what this experiment detects.

guide.title: Interference
steps: Write the Z-basis predictions for |+⟩ and |−⟩ before touching the code.
Toggle addPhase and run each preparation with direct readout. Record a pair of histograms.
Enable readInX and repeat. Use the sum and difference of amplitudes to account for the newly deterministic outcomes.

chapters.title: Boolean functions and feasibility
chapters.question: Can you undo a gate that copies one bit onto another?
chapters.activity: Trace the target bit through one controlled flip, then through a second.
chapters.objective: Build a gate you can run backwards. The test is whether you can recover both input bits from its output.
trace: Imagine a gate that writes x over a second bit y. Inputs 10 and 11 would both leave as 11. Seeing 11, you could never recover the old y. A reversible gate needs a distinct output for each input.

The statement if (x) { not(flag); } takes a different approach. When x is 0 it leaves flag alone. When x is 1 it flips flag. Try it on 10. One flip gives 11, and a second gives 10 again. This operation adds x to flag modulo two, usually written XOR.
chapters.exercise: Set mode to 0 and run once for each inputBit. Duplicate the controlled flip under the Uf comment. Predict the returned pair for each input before running again.
chapters.hint: The flag starts at false. Keep track of how many times it flips while x stays fixed.
chapters.solution: With one copy, inputs 0 and 1 return 00 and 11. With two copies, they return 00 and 10. The second copy restores the flag even for the input that changed it.
chapters.oral: If a reversible function counts as one oracle call, how much work did the computer do?
chapters.reason: One call counts a use of the function. To estimate the actual work, inspect how many gates, extra wires and successive steps its implementation needs.

chapters.title: Programming in Qiskit
chapters.question: How can you tell whether an exported circuit still runs your edited program?
chapters.activity: Change one gate in the playground and check the allowed pairs in the downloaded Python.
chapters.objective: Take a two-qubit program from Qutes to Qiskit. Use a prediction about the two results to check that the export carries your edit.
trace: The left qubit starts at 0. A Hadamard makes its measurement equally likely to be 0 or 1. The controlled flip connects the right qubit to it. The 00 branch stays put and the 10 branch becomes 11. Look at the two bits from a single shot. They always agree.

Run the program and open Circuit to find the two gates. Then open Qiskit Python. The downloaded file contains build_circuit(), which constructs the QuantumCircuit, and code that decodes the measured bits into the same order as the Qutes return line.
chapters.exercise: Leave readInX off and turn flipRight on. Predict the pairs, run the edit, and download its Python. With Qiskit and Aer installed, run python experiment.qiskit.py --shots 128 --seed 17. Compare the decoded pairs.
chapters.hint: Start with 00 and 11. Flip only the second bit of each pair.
chapters.solution: Both runs can produce 01 and 10. Neither should produce a matching pair. Different counts for 01 across the two runs are consistent with the same underlying probability of ½.
chapters.oral: What would make you investigate a difference between two simulators?
chapters.reason: A forbidden pair is a reason to check bit order and gates. A small difference in counts calls for more shots and a comparison of the estimated probabilities.

chapters.title: Quantum circuits
chapters.question: Could a shared coin imitate the measurements of a Bell pair?
chapters.activity: Read the pair once in the normal basis and once after a Hadamard on each wire.
chapters.objective: Test two explanations for matching bits. Compare a Bell circuit with a source that randomly hands you 00 or 11. Choose a readout on which their predictions differ.
trace: With flipRight off, the circuit prepares (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2. Direct measurement gives matching bits. A source that picked either 00 or 11 before each shot would produce the same counts.

Now turn on readInX. The two final Hadamards spread each starting branch over all four pairs. For 01 and 10, the contributions from the two Bell branches have opposite signs and cancel. A source that picked just one branch has nothing to cancel its contribution.
chapters.exercise: Predict the fraction of mismatched pairs for each source with readInX on. Run the Bell circuit and compare it with your calculation for the shared coin.
chapters.hint: Start the shared-coin calculation with 00. A Hadamard on each of those two qubits gives four equally likely pairs. Repeat the argument starting with 11.
chapters.solution: The Bell circuit still returns only 00 or 11. The shared coin would give all four pairs equally often in the long run, so its mismatch probability is ½.
chapters.oral: Why did the second readout teach you something the first could not?
chapters.reason: The two sources agreed on the first prediction. Changing the basis exposed interference between the Bell branches, which the randomly chosen classical pair cannot produce.

chapters.title: Special matrices
chapters.question: How many quarter turns bring a qubit back to its starting state?
chapters.activity: Change turns in the loop and predict when the final measurement is certain.
chapters.objective: Follow one amplitude through a loop. A few powers of the number i will tell you what the circuit can return.
trace: Each pass applies the phase gate S. Its matrix is diagonal with entries 1 and i. It leaves the amplitude for 0 alone and multiplies the amplitude for 1 by i. Starting after the first Hadamard, the relative factor goes from 1 to i, −1, −i and back to 1.
After k turns the final Hadamard gives outcome 0 an amplitude of (1 + iᵏ)/2. At two turns that is (1 − 1)/2, so false cannot occur. At four turns the two terms add again.
chapters.exercise: Set turns to 1, 2 and 4 in turn. Before each run, calculate the chance of false. Which setting has the same effect as skipping the loop?
chapters.hint: At one turn, the squared magnitude of 1 + i is 2. Remember to square the denominator as well.
chapters.solution: The probabilities of false are ½, 0 and 1. Four turns multiply the second amplitude by i⁴ = 1. Both entries of the state are back where they started.
chapters.oral: What if the phase gate acts on a qubit prepared entirely in state 1?
chapters.reason: Only one amplitude is occupied. Multiplying it by i gives the entire state a common phase, which leaves the probabilities of every later measurement unchanged.

chapters.title: Quantum oracles
chapters.question: How can a gate acting on the target leave a sign on the control?
chapters.activity: Compare the same controlled flip with three different preparations.
chapters.objective: Run the same oracle three ways. First use it to write a bit, then use it to reveal a phase on the wire that controls the flip.
trace: In mode 0, x holds inputBit and the flag starts at 0. The controlled flip writes x into the flag. With inputBit true, direct measurement therefore gives 11.

Modes 1 and 2 prepare x in |+⟩. Mode 1 prepares the flag in |+⟩ too. Swapping its two equal amplitudes changes nothing. Mode 2 prepares the flag in |−⟩. Swapping its opposite amplitudes gives the whole flag state a minus sign, but only on the branch where x is 1. That relative sign on x is phase kickback.
chapters.exercise: Keep inputBit true and predict the two returned bits for modes 1 and 2. Run both, then compare mode 2 with mode 0. What does the first bit tell you in each?
chapters.hint: In modes 1 and 2 both wires pass through a final Hadamard. It maps |+⟩ to 0 and |−⟩ to 1.
chapters.solution: Mode 1 gives 00. In mode 2 both wires reach the last Hadamards in |−⟩ and give 11. Mode 0 also prints 11, but its first bit is the input value. In mode 2 that bit reveals the sign acquired by the control.
chapters.oral: Could you detect kickback by measuring x before its final Hadamard?
chapters.reason: Both signs give equal chances of 0 and 1 in direct readout. The final gate lets the two amplitudes interfere, making their relative sign observable.

guide.title: Reversible oracles
steps: In mode 0, trace both inputBit settings through the controlled flip.
Compare modes 1 and 2. Both start with a superposed control. Write down the eigenvalue of X on each target.
Inspect the circuit to identify the query and final H gates. Use the two result fields to explain which wire carries evidence of kickback.

chapters.title: Auxiliary procedures
chapters.question: What happens if a helper qubit remembers which branch the circuit took?
chapters.activity: Compare the returned path and flag with eraseFlag on and off.
chapters.objective: Use a helper to apply a phase, then undo the computation that filled it. See why returning the helper to zero matters to the next gate.
trace: The first controlled flip copies the path bit into the flag. The two branches are now 00 and 11. A phase flip on the flag puts a minus sign on 11. The helper has done its job, but it still holds a record of the path.

With eraseFlag on, a second controlled flip takes 11 back to 10. Both branches now have flag 0, and their opposite signs remain on the path. The final Hadamard converts that sign difference into path 1.
chapters.exercise: Predict [path, flag] with eraseFlag on. Switch it off and predict which extra pairs can appear. Use Circuit to locate the gate that accounts for the difference.
chapters.hint: With the record intact, follow 00 and 11 separately through the Hadamard on the path. Their flag values stay different.
chapters.solution: Erasing gives 10 every time. Keeping the flag gives all four pairs with probability ¼ each. Branches with different flag values cannot cancel one another at the same joint outcome.
chapters.oral: Would measuring the flag and discarding the result work just as well?
chapters.reason: Measuring the flag selects a branch. Forgetting the result loses the record available to you, but it cannot restore the interference between the two original branches.

chapters.title: Elementary quantum algorithms
chapters.question: Can a circuit tell you whether two table entries differ?
chapters.activity: Write down a two-entry function and predict the circuit’s single output bit.
chapters.objective: Trace a small algorithm from preparation to answer. It asks one question about a whole truth table. Do its two entries agree?
trace: The switches describe a function of one bit. Its first entry, f(0), is offset. Its second, f(1), is offset XOR slope. For example, slope true and offset false give the table 0, 1. Flipping offset changes it to 1, 0.

The first Hadamards prepare both input branches and a target in |−⟩. The oracle puts a minus sign on each branch whose function value is 1. The final Hadamard returns false for equal signs and true for opposite signs.
chapters.exercise: Make four rows, one for each choice of slope and offset. Write f(0), f(1) and your predicted result in each row. Run the four settings to check your table.
chapters.hint: Changing offset flips both entries together. Ask whether that changes their agreement.
chapters.solution: The tables 00 and 11 both return false. The tables 01 and 10 both return true. The measured bit tells you the slope, while the offset remains unknown.
chapters.oral: After a true result, could you tell someone the value of f(0)?
chapters.reason: You know the entries differ. Both 01 and 10 fit that information, so either value of f(0) is still possible.

chapters.title: Quantum teleportation
chapters.question: How would Bob notice a missing teleportation correction?
chapters.activity: Remove the phase correction and compare two messages that react differently.
chapters.objective: Give Bob a way to test the state he receives. A missing correction is easy to overlook if you choose the wrong test message.
trace: Alice and Bob share a Bell pair. Alice couples the message to her half and measures two bits, zRecord and xRecord. Bob uses xRecord to decide whether to flip his qubit and zRecord to decide whether to flip its phase.

The last lines undo the known preparation of the test message. If Bob received it intact, that inverse takes his qubit back to 0. With phaseMessage off the message is |0⟩, which a phase flip leaves alone. With it on the message is |−⟩, which a phase flip turns into |+⟩.
chapters.exercise: Set correctPhase to false and try both messages. Read each output as [zRecord, xRecord, Bob’s test]. For which rows does the test catch an error?
chapters.hint: Removing the correction can matter only on a shot where zRecord asks for it.
chapters.solution: For |0⟩ the test still reads false on every shot. For |−⟩ it reads true precisely when zRecord is true. Restoring the correction brings the test back to false for both messages.
chapters.oral: If Alice sends just two classical bits, where does the ability to transfer an unknown state come from?
chapters.reason: The protocol also consumes a shared Bell pair. Alice’s bits tell Bob which operation will recover the state from his half. They do not describe the amplitudes, and Alice’s measurement consumes the original message.

guide.title: Teleportation and superdense coding
steps: Run teleportation for the phase message. Group the rows by Alice’s z record and check Bob’s verification bit.
Disable correctPhase. Compare the result for |−⟩ with the result for |0⟩. Identify the branches in which your test detects a fault.
Open the dense-coding experiment. Send 01 and 10, then compare the two protocols in terms of pre-shared entanglement, transmitted bits and transmitted qubits.

chapters.title: Superdense coding
chapters.question: How can sending one qubit deliver a two-bit message?
chapters.activity: Encode a pair of bits on Alice’s wire and predict what Bob’s two wires will read.
chapters.objective: Send the message 10 using a Bell pair. Follow where Bob finds each bit when he brings the two wires together.
trace: Alice and Bob start with a shared Bell pair. On her wire, Alice uses phaseBit to change the sign between 00 and 11. She uses flipBit to change whether the two bits agree. These two choices give four distinguishable joint states.
Alice sends her wire to Bob. His controlled flip puts the agreement information on kept. His final Hadamard turns the sign information into a bit on sent. The return line reads sent first, then kept.
chapters.exercise: Choose phaseBit true and flipBit false. Predict the pair, then try 01 and 11. Which measured wire changes when you edit only phaseBit?
chapters.hint: Work backwards from the last two gates. The Hadamard is on sent, and kept is the target of the controlled flip.
chapters.solution: The three choices decode to 10, 01 and 11. Changing only phaseBit changes the first measured bit. Bob’s original wire alone had equal chances of 0 and 1 for every message.
chapters.oral: What would you count when comparing this protocol with teleportation?
chapters.reason: Both consume a shared Bell pair. Dense coding sends one qubit to convey two chosen classical bits. Teleportation sends two classical bits to transfer the state of a qubit.

chapters.title: Deutsch’s algorithm
chapters.question: Why is one query enough for Deutsch’s decision?
chapters.activity: Follow two signs through the last gate and compare with reading one truth-table entry.
chapters.objective: Prove the decision rule you tested in the elementary algorithm. The proof fits in two amplitudes.
trace: Call the signs attached to the input branches u and v. Each is +1 for a function value of 0 and −1 for a value of 1. After one oracle call and the final Hadamard, the amplitudes for 0 and 1 are (u + v)/2 and (u − v)/2.

Take the table 1, 0. Its signs are −1, +1. Their sum vanishes, so the answer must be 1. Swapping the entries reverses both signs and still gives 1. For a constant table the difference vanishes instead.
chapters.exercise: Test all four tables with slope and offset. In the code, identify the block that changes target according to f(x). Which gates would still be needed if the oracle were supplied to you as a single operation?
chapters.hint: The two if statements between the preparation and the last Hadamard implement the chosen oracle.
chapters.solution: Both constant tables return false and both different-entry tables return true. Counting that middle block as one query still leaves preparation, the final Hadamard and measurement to perform.
chapters.oral: Could a service that accepts one classical input and replies with f(x) give the same guarantee?
chapters.reason: After seeing f(0), two possible tables can still disagree at f(1). The quantum algorithm needs a reversible oracle that preserves both input branches and their relative phase through the query.

chapters.title: Deutsch–Jozsa
chapters.question: Can one measurement separate a constant table from a balanced one?
chapters.activity: Count the positive and negative contributions to outcome 00.
chapters.objective: Move from two table entries to four. Under the promise that they are all equal or split evenly, one particular result tells you which case you have.
trace: One Hadamard on each input prepares the four strings with equal amplitudes. The oracle changes the sign for any string with function value 1. After the last Hadamards, the amplitude for 00 is the sum of those four signs divided by four.

Four matching signs give amplitude +1 or −1, so 00 is certain. Two signs of each kind cancel, so 00 is impossible. The balanced example uses high XOR low. Its signs in order are +, −, −, +, the pattern the last gates map to 11.
chapters.exercise: Try both values of balanced. For each one, predict whether turning on complement can change the measured pair. Then check all four settings.
chapters.hint: Complement reverses every sign together. What happens to the squared magnitude of their sum?
chapters.solution: Both constant settings return 00. Both parity settings return 11. The general decision uses 00 versus a nonzero result. The particular answer 11 comes from the parity function chosen here.
chapters.oral: If the promise were removed, what could you infer from a nonzero result?
chapters.reason: A constant function always gives 00, so a nonzero result rules it out. A table with three equal entries and one different entry could also give a nonzero result, so balance would need more evidence.

guide.title: Deutsch–Jozsa
steps: Build the four-entry sign table for the constant-zero function and for parity.
Predict the amplitude of 00 from the sum of the signs. Run both values of balanced.
Flip complement and run again. Explain how the query count can stay one even when the oracle contains multiple gates.

chapters.title: Simon’s algorithm
chapters.question: How can a random output rule out a hidden bit string?
chapters.activity: Use two independent measured strings to solve for the hidden mask.
chapters.objective: Recover a three-bit mask from clues. Each shot gives one equation about the mask, and different shots can give the same clue.
trace: The default oracle writes (high XOR low, mid) to its output. Inputs 000 and 101 therefore give the same value. In fact, flipping the outside two bits pairs every input with a partner. Call the mask joining partners s.

The final Hadamards make the two partners cancel for any measured string y whose dot product with s is odd. Each surviving y therefore tells you y · s = 0 modulo two. A sample of 010 says the middle mask bit is 0. A sample of 101 says the outside bits agree. With the promised nonzero mask, the only answer is 101.
chapters.exercise: Set alternate to true. Pick two independent nonzero rows from the results and write one equation for each. Check your candidate mask by finding two inputs with the same oracle output.
chapters.hint: For a row of 011, add the middle and low mask bits modulo two. A row of 100 tells you about the high bit alone.
chapters.solution: The allowed rows are 000, 011, 100 and 111. Their equations give high = 0 and mid = low. The nonzero solution is 011. Inputs 000 and 011 agree on both outputs of the alternate oracle.
chapters.oral: If you collect ten shots, have you necessarily collected enough information?
chapters.reason: Here you need two independent equations. A repeated row or 000 adds no information. Count independent constraints before deciding whether the mask is determined.

guide.title: Simon
steps: Collect output strings, retaining their high–middle–low order. Discard 000 and duplicate equations.
Pick two independent rows. Solve y·s=0 modulo two, and apply the nonzero-mask promise.
Enable alternate, derive the new mask, then find two different inputs on paper that the new oracle maps to the same output.

chapters.title: Shor’s algorithm
chapters.question: How does a repeating sequence lead to factors of 15?
chapters.activity: Turn a Fourier measurement into a candidate period, then test it using ordinary arithmetic.
chapters.objective: Factor 15 using a repeat in the powers of 2. The playground lets you study the quantum step that makes a period visible.
trace: Compute successive powers of 2 modulo 15. They are 1, 2, 4, 8 and 1. The first return to 1 takes four steps, so the order is r = 4. Halfway around, 2² = 4. Since (4 − 1)(4 + 1) = 15, taking the greatest common divisor of 15 with 3 and with 5 gives the two factors.

In the editor, the periodic input is supplied for you. The program prepares equal amplitudes at indices 1 and 5, four places apart in a register of size eight. It runs the inverse Fourier transform and measures. At output y the contributions differ in phase by 2π × 4y/8. For odd y they cancel. For even y they reinforce. The possible readings are 0, 2, 4 and 6.
Suppose you read 6. Reduce 6/8 to 3/4 and try the denominator, 4, as the period. Check that 2⁴ mod 15 = 1. A shot giving 4 instead suggests denominator 2, which fails the same check.
chapters.exercise: Reduce all four possible readings over eight. Which ones recover the order directly? Then turn on shorterPeriod, which prepares indices two places apart, and predict which peaks survive.
chapters.hint: A denominator is a candidate. Test it before using it to calculate factors. For the second experiment, ask which y makes 2y/8 a whole number.
chapters.solution: The fractions are 0/1, 1/4, 1/2 and 3/4. Readings 2 and 6 give order 4. With spacing two, the four input amplitudes reinforce only at 0 and 4. This second preparation models a different period.
chapters.oral: Which part of factoring did the browser demonstrate, and which part did you supply?
chapters.reason: The browser prepared selected indices and Fourier-sampled their spacing. You supplied the periodic input and checked the factors classically. A full order-finding circuit would first generate the periodic structure using controlled modular exponentiation.

chapters.title: Grover’s search
chapters.question: Why does changing the sign of one answer help you find it?
chapters.activity: Mark one of four strings and compare a sign flip alone with a full search step.
chapters.objective: Make one chosen answer certain in a four-item search. Follow its amplitude through the two operations that do the work.
trace: The first Hadamards give 00, 01, 10 and 11 amplitude ½ each. By default the oracle marks 10. It changes that amplitude to −½. Measuring now would still give each string probability ¼ because the four magnitudes are equal.

Diffusion reflects each amplitude around their mean, now ¼. For an unmarked answer, 2 × ¼ − ½ = 0. For the marked answer, 2 × ¼ − (−½) = 1. The gate sequence can add a common sign, which leaves these probabilities unchanged.
chapters.exercise: Set markHigh false and markLow true to search for 01. Predict the results with diffuse off and on. Export the amplified circuit from Qiskit Python. If a hardware run includes 00, what would you check first?
chapters.hint: Keep the mark fixed and change only diffusion. On hardware, a known input with a single 1 makes it easier to check which output bit is which.
chapters.solution: Without diffusion all four answers are equally likely. With it, the ideal circuit returns only 01. For hardware, check bit order with a known input, inspect the compiled two-qubit gates and depth, and compare the fraction of 01 over repeated shots with the ideal prediction.
chapters.oral: Does a smaller number of oracle calls guarantee a faster hardware run?
chapters.reason: Query count describes uses of the oracle. Actual time and accuracy also depend on implementing that oracle, routing gates, noise and the shots needed to identify the answer.

guide.title: Grover
steps: Mark 10. Write the four amplitudes immediately after the oracle, then calculate their mean.
Turn off diffuse. Check whether the phase mark alone changes the histogram. Restore diffusion and mark 01.
Inspect and export the edited circuit. Identify the marking and reflection stages, then propose a control for a noisy hardware run.

extensions.title: The CHSH game
extensions.question: How often can Alice and Bob win a game without exchanging their questions?
extensions.activity: Play all four pairs of settings and compare the average win rate with three wins in four.
extensions.objective: Try a game with a simple rule. Alice and Bob must give matching answers unless both questions are 1. In that case their answers must differ.
trace: Suppose they agree on a list of answers before playing. Matching on questions 00, 01 and 10 forces all four entries on their lists to be equal. They must then lose on 11. Always answering 0 achieves three wins out of four equally likely questions. Mixing different lists cannot raise that average.

With a Bell pair they can choose a measurement direction for each question. Alice uses 0° or 90°, and Bob uses +45° or −45°. The correlation is the cosine of the angle between the directions. For each question pair, the chance of the required match or mismatch is (1 + 1/√2)/2, about 85.4%.
extensions.exercise: Run the four combinations of xSetting and ySetting with the same number of shots. The program returns true for a win. Find the win fraction for each pair, then average the four fractions.
extensions.hint: Weight the four questions equally. Looking only at the setting with the most wins would change the game.
extensions.solution: The ideal average is about 85.4%, above the classical limit of 75%. Your finite sample can fall on either side of the ideal prediction. Repeating an identical run with the same simulator seed repeats its sample.
extensions.oral: What would a physical test need to show beyond these simulator counts?
extensions.reason: It would need independent setting choices, separated measurements and a statistical treatment of missed detections and sampling uncertainty. A simulator lets you check the predicted correlations under the model.

extensions.title: BB84 basis sifting
extensions.question: Which transmissions should Alice and Bob keep for a key?
extensions.activity: Compare matching and mismatched measurement choices, then introduce Eve’s probe.
extensions.objective: Send the same bit several ways. Decide which rounds give Bob a predictable answer and which could expose a disturbance.
trace: With aliceX and bobX both true, Alice applies a Hadamard to encode her bit and Bob applies another to read it. The two gates undo each other. If only one of them uses a Hadamard, Bob has a 50% chance of each result. After comparing their basis choices publicly, they keep the matching rounds. This selection is called sifting.

Turn on interceptZ. Eve’s probe now records the signal in the Z basis. A signal prepared in Z still carries the same bit. For a signal prepared in X, the probe leaves a record of its Z component, so Bob’s final Hadamard can no longer recover the encoded bit with certainty.
extensions.exercise: Leave bit true. Try matched Z, matched X and one mismatched pair with the probe off. Turn it on and repeat the matched rounds. Which retained rounds can now give Bob false?
extensions.hint: In this experiment Eve always probes in Z. Compare that choice with the basis Alice and Bob used in each retained round.
extensions.solution: Without the probe both matched rounds give true. With the probe, matched Z still gives true, but matched X gives false half the time. If half the retained rounds use X, the overall error probability is ½ × ½ = ¼.
extensions.oral: If Alice and Bob find one wrong bit on a real channel, what can they conclude?
extensions.reason: One bit shows a disagreement. Noise can also cause errors. They compare a sample of retained bits to estimate the error rate and decide whether they can safely use the remaining data.

extensions.title: Bernstein–Vazirani
extensions.question: Can one query reveal all three bits of a hidden mask?
extensions.activity: Change one mask bit and follow the sign change on the corresponding wire.
extensions.objective: Recover a mask from a function that returns just one bit for each ordinary input. The structure of the function lets the circuit read one coefficient on each wire.
trace: The function returns the parity of the input bits selected by the mask. With mask 101 it adds the high and low bits modulo two. The phase oracle gives a minus sign to the inputs whose selected bits have odd parity.

Each input wire begins in |+⟩. The sign pattern above is exactly what you get by applying a phase flip on each selected wire. Those wires become |−⟩. The last Hadamards turn |−⟩ into 1 and |+⟩ into 0, so the return line reads the mask in high, middle, low order.
extensions.exercise: Predict the output with the default mask. Set maskLow to false and predict again. Compare the meaning of one measured string here with one measured string in Simon’s experiment.
extensions.hint: Only the wire whose flag changed loses its phase flip. The other two finish as before.
extensions.solution: The default gives 101 and the edit gives 100. Here each measured bit is a coefficient of the mask. In Simon’s algorithm one measured string instead supplies one equation that the mask must satisfy.
extensions.oral: How can a one-query algorithm return a three-bit string?
extensions.reason: The promise restricts the oracle to binary linear functions. One coherent application gives the whole input register a sign pattern determined by those three coefficients. The final gates decode that pattern onto three measured wires.
